scripts.opening:opening:
[mischievously] JAUNT: THE SISTERS OF THE LEVEE. Dusk on a Monday in November 1904, at Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

Four stops, walking west from Millionaire's Row toward the Levee, the city's red-light district, and ending at a church on its edge. [short pause] [conspiratorially] Prairie Avenue is three blocks from the most famous address in Chicago, [amused] and it is not the Glessner House. Two sisters who called themselves Everleigh opened a club on Dearborn Street in 1900, and the richest men in the world have found their way to it.

[short pause] Start at the corner. [whispers] Watch which way the cabs turn.
scripts.stop:corner: [conspiratorially] Eighteenth and Prairie, as the lamps come on. [short pause] Eighteenth Street is a border. To the north and east: the mansions. To the south and west, "several blocks away from Prairie Avenue", begins the Levee, the district that runs from Eighteenth Street to Twenty-second, Wabash to Clark, home of the city's most famous brothels. [short pause] [primly] The ladies of Prairie Avenue never mention it. [short pause] [amused] And yet one of the two most famous houses in Chicago, Vic Shaw's, stood for a time on Prairie Avenue itself. [short pause] [whispers] The two gentlemen hurrying round this corner are not going home. [mischievously] Follow them west.
scripts.stop:sisters: [intrigued] Indiana Avenue, a block west. Keep walking and in three more blocks there is Dearborn Street, and at 2131 and 2133 Dearborn, the Everleigh Club. Its owners are two sisters, Ada and Minna. [short pause] [amused] They say they are from Kentucky; that was "another story concocted by the sisters". [short pause] They were born Simms, in Virginia, in 1864 and 1866. With about $35,000 they ran a house in Omaha, then came to Chicago and bought out a madam's house on Dearborn. [short pause] [warmly] They took a new name from their grandmother, who signed her letters "Everly yours". The club opened on 1 February 1900, and on the first night they turned many callers away. [long pause] [knowingly] In this business, the Everleighs understood, saying no is how you make a price.
scripts.stop:rooms: [amused] Further south along Indiana, with the Levee two blocks west. [short pause] [impressed] Inside the Everleigh Club are fifty rooms across two mansions: a Japanese Throne Room, a Mirror Room, a Silver Parlor, "a $15,000 gold-leafed piano for the Music Room" and "$650 gold cuspidors". [short pause] [incredulous] A bottle of champagne costs $12, "in an era when an entire meal could be had for fifty cents", and the entrance fee alone is $50. [short pause] Ada keeps the books and hires the women. Minna meets the guests. [short pause] [mischievously] In March 1902 Prince Henry of Prussia came, and when a slipper flew off during a dance and spilled champagne, one of his party drank from it, [laughs] and a whole custom began. The club keeps 15 to 25 cooks and maids, and its women are called "butterflies".
scripts.stop:church: [wryly] First Presbyterian Church, at Indiana and Twenty-first Street. [short pause] It stands at the Levee's eastern edge, close enough to hear it on a summer night. [short pause] [conspiratorially] The club's famed clients, the stories say, include the actor John Barrymore and the authors Ring Lardner and Theodore Dreiser, and gossips name the young Marshall Field Jr., who lives a few blocks from here, among them. "A rival madam maliciously accused the Everleigh sisters" of far worse, later, and the rumour never died. [long pause] The minister's door is lit. [short pause] So is the club's. [short pause] [amused] Tonight, as every night, the Levee is busier.
scripts.ending:close: [measured] End of the walk. The Everleigh Club lasted eleven years. On 24 October 1911 the mayor, Carter Harrison Jr., ordered it closed, [amused] and Minna took it the way she took everything: "If the Mayor says we must close, that settles it...I'll close up shop and walk out with a smile on my face." [short pause] The building was razed in July 1933. [long pause] [wryly] Prairie Avenue never once admitted that it knew the way to Dearborn Street. [short pause] [chuckles] It only ever knew the way back.
